passage: I'm Wasim, and last term maths felt like sand slipping through my fingers. Numbers wouldn't stay put. If Ammi said "Be back by quarter to six," I didn't know what that looked like on the clock. In class, when Arnab Sir said "Quick, how many minutes till lunch?", my chest went tight and my mind went white. But I could draw anything. My notebook margins were full of horses. Then Arnab Sir stopped asking me quick questions in front of everyone. He gave me a cardboard clock with hands I could move, and we counted in fives with bottle caps, again and again, no scolding. Now I can find quarter to six. I drew a horse on that cardboard clock, right at the six.

qa.q: What did Arnab Sir give Wasim to practise with?
qa.a: A cardboard clock with hands Wasim could move.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when asked a quick maths question in class, and what shows it?
qa.a: Panic; Wasim's chest went tight and Wasim's mind went white.

qa.q: Which change by Arnab Sir made progress possible?
qa.a: He stopped the quick public questions and used hands-on things like the clock and bottle caps, repeating patiently without scolding.

qa.q: How might Arnab Sir see Wasim's horse drawing on the clock?
qa.a: He may see it as a sign that Wasim now feels safe and even proud around the clock that once caused panic.

grounding: It shows a child who struggles with time and numbers and panics in maths though good at art, helped by hands-on materials, repetition and no shaming.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4B, class shop week Rafiq priced the pencils beautifully; his labels had drawings of each item. But when Mehak bought an eraser for seven rupees with a ten-rupee coin, Rafiq froze. He counted the coins in the box three times, went red and whispered, "I can't do it." He left the counter and hid in the reading corner. In writing time the same afternoon he wrote a funny story about a shopkeeper parrot, full of lively words. What I did next: I gave Rafiq a tray of real coins and a number line, and we practised change privately, one small amount a day. No one is timed at the shop now. By Friday he gave three rupees change, checked it twice, and grinned. - Madhuri, class teacher

qa.q: How much did the eraser cost in the class shop?
What does Rafiq hiding in the reading corner suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt panic and embarrassment when he couldn't work out the change in front of others.

qa.q: What small steps did Madhuri take that helped Rafiq?
qa.a: Madhuri gave him real coins and a number line, practised privately one small amount a day, and stopped timing children at the shop.

qa.q: How might Mehak have been affected if Madhuri had scolded Rafiq at the counter?
qa.a: Mehak and the other children might have learned to see Rafiq as slow, and his shame would have grown.

grounding: A teacher sees a child who panics over money though he is strong in writing, and uses hands-on coins and patient repetition without shaming.
